Lead integrations: Workiz lists Angi, Thumbtack and Yelp integrations, Contractor+ lists Angi and Thumbtack, and Housecall Pro lists Thumbtack; Jobber can connect other tools through Zapier.

Time and materials: if you bill by the hour, test time entry on the phone and a time-and-materials invoice during each trial.

Photos: before and after photos show the problem and the finished work.

Mobile workflow: run a real job through each tool's mobile app, from quote to payment.
verticals.regulatory_notes:
Rules that affect what handyman software should record:

Contractor licensing: some states exempt small jobs below a dollar threshold from contractor licensing, and a license applies above it. Check your state's threshold before you quote larger jobs.

Trade licenses: electrical, plumbing and HVAC work can require a trade license, depending on the state, so check the scope of each job against your licenses.

Insurance: keep certificates of general liability and, if you have employees, workers' compensation where office staff can send them.

Employment records: US employers must complete Form I-9 for every hire.

vertical_faqs.q: Which handyman software fits a solo operator?
vertical_faqs.a: Contractor+, Jobber and Joist are places to start. Contractor+ has a free Freedom plan (up to 5 estimates or invoices a month) and Pro at $29 a month billed monthly. Joist is quotes and invoices from $8.34 a month billed annually or $10 billed monthly (Basics, up to 5 documents a month); its Run plan ($100 a month list, offered at an introductory 30% off) adds jobs and scheduling. Jobber (Core from $29 a month billed annually) adds scheduling and a client portal, with automated quote and invoice follow-ups from the Connect plan up.

vertical_faqs.q: How do handyman operators handle lead-gen platforms (TaskRabbit, Thumbtack, Angi)?
vertical_faqs.a: Check which platforms each tool connects to, so leads arrive as jobs without retyping: Workiz lists Angi, Thumbtack and Yelp, Contractor+ lists Angi and Thumbtack, Housecall Pro lists Thumbtack, and Jobber can connect other tools through Zapier. None of the tools in our data lists a TaskRabbit integration. Track bookings by lead source to see what each platform costs you per job.

vertical_faqs.q: Can handyman software handle multi-trade work (plumbing + electrical + carpentry)?
vertical_faqs.a: General tools such as Jobber and Housecall Pro list handyman work among their trades and can schedule and invoice any job type. The bigger question is licensing: some states exempt small jobs below a dollar threshold from contractor licensing, and electrical, plumbing and HVAC work can need a trade license, so check each job's scope against your licenses.

vertical_faqs.q: Should handyman operations use flat-rate pricing or time-and-materials?
vertical_faqs.a: Time and materials suits jobs whose scope is hard to predict; a set price suits repeatable jobs such as a fixture install. Check that your tool handles both: fixed quotes, and hourly time entry with materials on the invoice.

vertical_faqs.q: When should a handyman operation move to a specialized trade FSM?
vertical_faqs.a: If one trade becomes most of your work, compare the tools on that trade's page with what you use now. Trade-specific features (memberships in HVAC, flat-rate pricebooks in plumbing, permit tracking in electrical) matter more once that trade drives your business.

verticals.name: Solar
verticals.industry_context:
Residential solar is sold on a proposal: system size, panel layout, production estimate, savings and financing, presented to the homeowner. That makes design, proposal and sales software the core of a solar company's stack, with dispatch a smaller part. Design tools such as Aurora Solar and OpenSolar build 3D site models and production estimates from imagery; Solo builds in-home proposals, with the option of having Solo's team do the design; and Enerflo connects sales, design, financing, contracts and installation tracking in one workflow.

When a deal is financed, the proposal has to show lenders' monthly payments. Aurora, OpenSolar, Solo and Enerflo all list lender integrations, including GoodLeap and LightReach.

What happens after the sale matters too. A proposal the install team cannot build as sold leads to change orders, so check how each tool's design carries into engineering and permitting: Aurora sells permit-ready plan sets and engineering stamps as add-ons, Solargraf generates permit plan sets, OpenSolar builds single-line diagrams, and Solo does not advertise plan sets.
verticals.feature_priorities:
Features to test for solar work:

Design speed and accuracy: roof modeling from satellite or LIDAR imagery and a production estimate. Solo detects rooflines with AI; Aurora lists AI-assisted site models under its Enterprise plan.

Financing: the proposal should show monthly payment options from several lenders. Aurora, OpenSolar, Solo and Enerflo list lender integrations such as GoodLeap and LightReach.

Editing in the conversation: reps need to change system size, equipment and pricing with the homeowner.

Permit-ready output: single-line diagrams, wire sizing and voltage drop. Aurora sells permit-ready plan sets and engineering stamps as paid add-ons, Solargraf generates permit plan sets, Pylon generates single-line diagrams and voltage rise reports, OpenSolar builds single-line diagrams but does not mention wire sizing or stamps, and Solo does not advertise plan sets.

Lead to installation: Enerflo connects sales, contracts, financing and install tracking on top of your design tool.

vertical_faqs.q: What kinds of software do solar installers use?
vertical_faqs.a: Design-and-proposal tools on this page differ in approach. Aurora Solar offers 3D design, proposals and permit plan sets on published per-user plans (from $135 per user per month billed annually, or $159 month to month); Solargraf (owned by Enphase) offers design, proposals with financing and permit plan sets on annual plans (from $2,799 a year for 2 users and 240 projects); OpenSolar is free to use (no licence fee, with API access, connectors and premium imagery charged separately); Solo focuses on fast in-home proposals, with the option of having Solo's team build the design (quote-based pricing); and Enerflo connects sales, design, financing and install tracking in one lead-to-installation platform. Pick by whether you want free (OpenSolar), in-house design with permit plan sets (Aurora or Solargraf), outsourced design (Solo), or a full operations platform (Enerflo).

vertical_faqs.q: Is OpenSolar really free?
vertical_faqs.a: Yes. OpenSolar's design, sales and project management software has no licence fee for installers; OpenSolar says its hardware, finance and service partners pay to be part of the platform instead. Since April 2026 it has charged for API access (per project) and for connectors such as Xero and QuickBooks (a monthly subscription), and premium imagery is bought per image, but the core platform is still free. Because partners pay for placement, the lenders and products you see first in the app are OpenSolar's commercial partners.

vertical_faqs.q: Which solar tools produce permit-ready plan sets?
vertical_faqs.a: Some solar tools are built around the sales proposal (layout, production, savings) rather than stamped engineering, so permit-ready single-line diagrams, wire sizing and voltage-drop calculations can come from separate services or add-ons. Aurora sells permit-ready plan sets (single-line or three-line diagrams with conductor sizes) and engineering stamps as paid add-ons, Solargraf generates permit plan sets from the same account as its designs and proposals, Pylon generates editable single-line diagrams and voltage rise reports from its designs, OpenSolar builds single-line diagrams but does not mention wire sizing or stamps, and Solo's pages do not advertise plan sets. If permit-ready output matters to your workflow, test the electrical design depth specifically.

verticals.name: Moving
verticals.industry_context:
A moving company's work runs from lead and quote (by weight, volume, distance or hours) through crew and truck scheduling to the job itself: an electronic bill of lading (eBOL), an inventory of the customer's goods, and payment. Moving platforms such as SmartMoving, Supermove, MoveitPro, Elromco, Moveware and Network Leads are built for that workflow, including local, intrastate and interstate moves, crew apps, storage and eBOL.

Some of these platforms also cover sales follow-up: SmartMoving and Network Leads list automated follow-ups, and Supermove's AI Sales Copilot shows live checklists during calls and drafts follow-ups.

For accounting, SmartMoving, Supermove, Elromco and Network Leads list QuickBooks integrations, and Moveware includes its own accounting package.
verticals.feature_priorities:
Features to test for moving companies:

Quoting: local (hourly) and long-distance (weight or volume) pricing, plus an online quote form that captures leads. Elromco's online quote forms show customers a price on the spot.

Lead follow-up: automated follow-ups and call tools. SmartMoving, Network Leads and Supermove all list them.

Crew and truck scheduling: assigning crew size and trucks to each job on a dispatch board.

On the job: an electronic bill of lading, inventory capture and a crew app that collects signatures, photos and payments. MoveitPro's crew app costs $20 per crew user a month, and Elromco's crew portal is a mobile web app rather than a native app.

Payments, storage and accounting: deposits, balance on delivery, storage billing, and QuickBooks or built-in accounting.

vertical_faqs.q: What software do moving companies use?
vertical_faqs.a: Moving companies can choose from platforms built for moving. SmartMoving (for moving and storage companies, including multi-location and franchise operators) and Supermove (office, crew, estimator and storage apps plus AI sales tools) cover CRM, dispatch and crew apps; MoveitPro was built by a moving company owner who began writing it in 2011 and includes a crew app and AI call tools; Elromco is an all-in-one for small and mid-size movers with published prices; Moveware is an ERP for mid-size and larger moving, relocation and storage companies; and Network Leads combines a moving CRM with the leads it sells.

vertical_faqs.q: How much does moving company software cost?
vertical_faqs.a: Elromco publishes its prices (Professional $289 a month for 3 office users, Enterprise $399), and Network Leads lists Starter at $249 and Growth at $399 a month, with leads billed separately. SmartMoving, Supermove, MoveitPro and Moveware publish no base prices, so you need a quote; MoveitPro does list its crew app at $20 per crew user per month.

vertical_faqs.q: Do movers need dedicated software, or will general FSM work?
vertical_faqs.a: Some general field service tools list moving among the trades they serve, but the moving-specific workflow (weight and volume long-distance quoting, eBOL, valuation, crew-size dispatch, storage) is what the moving platforms are built around. If you do long-distance or interstate moves or run storage, test those workflows before choosing a general tool.

verticals.name: Restoration
verticals.industry_context:
Restoration covers water, fire, mold and storm damage, and when a job is paid by insurance, that shapes the software. An insurance job needs evidence the carrier and adjuster will accept: photos, moisture readings, drying logs and contents lists. Xactimate (Verisk) is estimating software used by insurance carriers and adjusters, so its integrations matter across the category. Jobs also follow a mitigation-then-repair sequence and include emergency calls at any hour.

The tools split into two roles. Encircle is a field documentation tool: photos, moisture maps, drying logs and contents captured on a phone and organized into carrier-ready reports. Albi, DASH, PSA and Restoration Manager are job-management platforms that run scheduling, equipment tracking, Xactimate or XactAnalysis links, accounting and job financials. Some restorers run a documentation tool and a job-management platform together; Encircle's integration list includes Albi and PSA.
verticals.feature_priorities:
Features to test for restoration work:

Field documentation: photos, moisture mapping, drying logs and contents capture that a carrier will accept. Encircle is built around this, and Albi lists moisture mapping and drying logs.

Xactimate and XactAnalysis: Encircle's Scope to Estimate drafts an Xactimate estimate from field data, Albi and Restoration Manager list Xactimate and XactAnalysis integrations, PSA lists both, and DASH syncs XactAnalysis notes but does not describe an Xactimate estimate import on its current pages.

Job management: scheduling crews through mitigation and repair, plus emergency dispatch.

Equipment tracking: air movers, dehumidifiers and air scrubbers on a job are billable and easy to lose. Albi, DASH, PSA and Restoration Manager list equipment tracking.

Accounting and job financials: Albi, DASH and Restoration Manager list QuickBooks integrations, and PSA includes full accounting.

Mobile and offline: documentation happens on site, so test the mobile app where the signal is weak; Encircle says its app works fully offline.

vertical_faqs.q: What software do restoration companies use?
vertical_faqs.a: Restoration platforms come in two kinds, and some restorers run one of each: a field documentation tool such as Encircle for carrier-ready photos, moisture maps and drying logs, and a job management platform such as Albi, DASH, PSA or Restoration Manager for scheduling, equipment tracking, Xactimate or XactAnalysis links, accounting and job financials. Encircle's integration list includes Albi and PSA.

vertical_faqs.q: How much does restoration software cost?
vertical_faqs.a: Albi charges $60 a month per field seat and $100 per office seat, with a $6,000 minimum annual subscription. Encircle prices documentation by jobs per year, from $285 a month for up to 200 jobs on a 12-month term, with unlimited users. Restoration Manager, DASH and PSA publish no prices, so you need a quote. If you pay for both a documentation tool and a job management platform, compare the combined cost.

vertical_faqs.q: Why is documentation so important in restoration software?
vertical_faqs.a: Because insurance carriers pay claims on evidence: photos, moisture readings and drying logs support the claim. Field documentation tools such as Encircle capture that evidence on site, and integration with Xactimate, the estimating software carriers and adjusters use, links the documentation to the estimate.

verticals.name: Painting
verticals.industry_context:
A painting job starts with a quote, and painters price by surface area and surface type (walls, trim, ceilings, interior or exterior, prep and paint). That is why the painting-specific tools on this page center on estimating and proposals.

Painting tools on this page take two approaches. PaintScout prices from your own production rates for each surface and turns estimates into proposals, and Estimate Rocket is a multi-trade estimating and project tool. CorkCRM is a painting CRM that adds lead tracking, scheduling, crew timecards and invoices, and QuoteIQ is a multi-trade all-in-one with a paint calculator, AI before and after images, satellite measurement and review requests. General tools such as Jobber and Housecall Pro list painting among their trades.
verticals.feature_priorities:
Features to test for painting work:

Surface-based estimating: pricing by square footage and surface type, ideally from your own production rates. PaintScout works out labor and materials from the rates you set, and QuoteIQ includes a paint calculator on every plan.

Proposals: branded proposals with options the customer can pick and an e-signature. PaintScout, CorkCRM and Estimate Rocket include e-signatures.

Lead follow-up: automated follow-ups on unsold quotes. PaintScout's Sales plan includes automated email and text follow-ups, and Estimate Rocket runs follow-up campaigns.

Scheduling and crews: CorkCRM schedules jobs and crews with timecards, and PaintScout adds scheduling through its Operations add-on.

Reviews: QuoteIQ includes review management.

Measuring: QuoteIQ's MapMeasure Pro measures walls, roofs, decks, fences and driveways from satellite imagery, from its Beginner plan.

vertical_faqs.q: What software do painting contractors use?
vertical_faqs.a: Painters can choose painting-focused tools or general ones. PaintScout is built for painter estimating (production-rate pricing and proposals), and CorkCRM is a painting CRM that adds lead tracking, scheduling, crew timecards and invoices. QuoteIQ (with a paint calculator and review management) and Estimate Rocket are multi-trade tools that serve painters. Jobber and Housecall Pro list painting among their trades.

vertical_faqs.q: How much does painting software cost?
vertical_faqs.a: QuoteIQ starts at $29.99 a month for 1 user. PaintScout's Sales plan is $99 a month billed annually ($119 monthly) with 1 user, plus $20 per extra user and $79 a month billed annually for the Operations add-on. CorkCRM runs from $149 a month for 1 user to $349 for unlimited users, and Estimate Rocket from $139 a month with 3 full users to $359 with 15. Check how each price scales with the number of estimators you need.

vertical_faqs.q: Do painters need dedicated software or will general FSM work?
vertical_faqs.a: General field service tools such as Jobber and Housecall Pro list painting among their trades and cover scheduling, invoicing and payments. Painting estimating software such as PaintScout prices jobs by surface and your production rates and produces painter-specific proposals, and QuoteIQ adds a paint calculator and AI before and after images. If estimating speed and accuracy are your bottleneck, trial a painting tool alongside a general one.

verticals.name: Flooring
verticals.industry_context:
Flooring jobs are priced from a material takeoff, and seams, pattern repeat, dye lots, remnants and waste all change how much material a job uses. Stores also carry roll goods and remnants in inventory. That is why flooring has its own software rather than relying on general field service tools.

The tools split by role. MeasureSquare is a takeoff and estimating specialist (roll layouts, seam diagrams, cut sheets). RFMS, QFloors and RollMaster are dealer systems that run point of sale, roll-goods inventory, ordering, scheduling and accounting in one system. Floorzap is an all-in-one for independent flooring retailers that keeps QuickBooks for accounting, and Broadlume leads with websites, marketing and room visualization.

QFloors ties into room visualization: Roomvo, the room visualization company, bought QFloors in January 2025, and the two sell combined bundles.
verticals.feature_priorities:
Features to test for flooring work:

Takeoff accuracy: seam, pattern-repeat and waste logic, and roll layouts. MeasureSquare is built for this.

Inventory: rolls, remnants, dye lots and special orders. RFMS, QFloors and RollMaster include inventory; RollMaster lists real-time inventory valuation and warehouse barcoding.

Job costing: RFMS (batch job costing on its higher packages), QFloors, RollMaster and Floorzap list job costing.

Point of sale, quoting and ordering: the dealer systems handle order entry and purchasing.

Scheduling installs: Floorzap schedules measures, deliveries and installs, and gives installers a bilingual portal on their phones.

Accounting: QFloors and RollMaster are sold as replacements for QuickBooks; MeasureSquare and Floorzap integrate with QuickBooks.

Room visualization: Broadlume includes a flooring visualizer, and QFloors sells bundles with Roomvo.

vertical_faqs.q: What software do flooring dealers use?
vertical_faqs.a: Flooring has its own tools. MeasureSquare is a takeoff and estimating specialist (takeoffs, roll layouts and seam diagrams), while RFMS, QFloors and RollMaster are dealer systems that run point of sale, roll-goods inventory, ordering, scheduling and accounting. Floorzap is an all-in-one for independent retailers, and Broadlume leads with websites and marketing. MeasureSquare connects to QFloors, RollMaster and QuickBooks Online (its QuickBooks Online link is labeled beta), so it can pair with a dealer system or QuickBooks for the back office.

vertical_faqs.q: How much does flooring software cost?
vertical_faqs.a: MeasureSquare publishes per-user prices by product, from $54 to $197 a month on monthly billing for a single product (less on annual billing). Floorzap starts at $399 a month plus a one-time setup fee, and QFloors at $89 per user per month plus a one-time setup fee. RFMS, RollMaster (now sold as Broadlume's business management software) and Broadlume's websites and marketing publish no prices, so you need a quote.

vertical_faqs.q: Do I need a full ERP or just estimating software?
vertical_faqs.a: It depends on where you lose time and money. If the bottleneck is fast, accurate takeoffs, an estimating specialist like MeasureSquare plus QuickBooks may be enough. If you are losing track of inventory, orders and margin across the store, or run several locations, a dealer system (QFloors, RFMS or RollMaster) brings them together but costs more and takes setup. A takeoff tool and a dealer system can also run together: MeasureSquare connects to QFloors and RollMaster.

vertical_faqs.q: Does flooring software include room visualization?
vertical_faqs.a: Some does. Roomvo, the room visualization company, bought QFloors in January 2025 and the two sell combined bundles, and Broadlume includes a flooring visualizer on its websites and in-store visualization in its Retail Selling System. If showroom and online selling matter to you, weigh visualization alongside back-office features.

verticals.name: Waste & Junk Removal
verticals.industry_context:
Waste and junk businesses run on trucks, drivers, recurring schedules and physical assets (tanks, portable toilets, dumpsters, containers) that get placed, serviced and picked up. The software is built around scheduling and dispatch, routing, tracking where each container is, and recurring billing.

The tools split by segment. ServiceCore is built for portable restroom, septic (including grease trap) and roll-off dumpster operators; Docket, a ServiceCore company, for roll-off dumpster rental and junk removal; Starlight Software for waste and recycling companies with several lines of business; Trash Flow for haulers, landfills and transfer stations that buy Windows software in modules; and Routeware for private haulers and city or county collection fleets. Bin Boss, iCANS and Roll-Off Amigo are dumpster rental apps for smaller roll-off companies.

Residential junk removal is closer to standard scheduling, dispatch and invoicing, and general field service tools such as Workiz, Housecall Pro and Jobber list it among their trades.
verticals.feature_priorities:
Features to test for waste and junk removal:

Scheduling and dispatch: assigning drop-offs, pickups, swaps and service visits to trucks and drivers, and changing them during the day.

Routing: Routeware, ServiceCore and iCANS list route optimization, Docket's IronRouteAI route creation is in its top plan, and Trash Flow sells route optimization as a monthly add-on.

Container and asset tracking: where each dumpster, portable toilet or tank is placed and when it is due. ServiceCore maps placed units, Docket records container locations with PIN or QR scans, and Bin Boss, iCANS and Trash Flow track containers.

Recurring billing and payments: automated invoicing, online payments and a customer portal. Bin Boss also compares weight tickets with each dumpster's allowance and creates overage charges for review.

Driver app: turn-by-turn directions, photos, signatures and offline use. ServiceCore's and Docket's driver apps work offline.

Accounting: ServiceCore, Docket, Bin Boss and iCANS sync with QuickBooks Online.

vertical_faqs.q: What software do junk removal, dumpster, and septic businesses use?
vertical_faqs.a: It depends on the segment. ServiceCore is built for portable restroom, septic and roll-off dumpster operators; Docket and Starlight Software for roll-off and hauling; Bin Boss, iCANS and Roll-Off Amigo for smaller dumpster rental companies; Trash Flow for haulers and landfills that want modular Windows software; and Routeware for private haulers and city or county collection fleets. Residential junk removal crews can also use general field service tools such as Workiz, Housecall Pro or Jobber, which list junk removal among their trades.

vertical_faqs.q: How much does waste/junk removal software cost?
vertical_faqs.a: Prices vary by model. ServiceCore charges per truck on an annual contract and Docket sells three plans, but neither publishes plan prices, and Starlight and Routeware publish none either. Trash Flow publishes one-time module prices (for example $3,600 for its billing bundle with container tracking) plus monthly add-ons. Bin Boss and iCANS list flat plans from $99 a month, and Roll-Off Amigo has a free tier. Among general tools used for junk removal, Jobber starts at $29 a month billed annually and Housecall Pro at $59, while Workiz quotes on request.

vertical_faqs.q: Do I need dedicated waste software or a generalist field-service tool?
vertical_faqs.a: It comes down to whether you manage placed assets and routes or mostly one-off jobs. If you place and track containers (dumpsters, portable toilets) or run recurring routes, a dedicated platform (ServiceCore, Docket, Starlight, Trash Flow or a dumpster rental app) is built for that. If you run a residential junk-removal crew whose needs are scheduling, dispatch and invoicing, a general field service tool may cover them.

vertical_faqs.q: Why does asset and container tracking matter so much?
vertical_faqs.a: For dumpster, portable toilet and septic businesses, the containers and tanks are what you rent and service. Knowing where each unit is placed, how long it has been out and when it is due for service prevents lost or unbilled units, which is why the dedicated waste platforms track units by location.

verticals.name: Fire Protection & Life Safety
verticals.industry_context:
Fire protection and life safety is commercial service work built around inspections. Inspecting and servicing sprinklers, fire alarms, extinguishers, suppression systems, backflow preventers, and fire doors and dampers follows codes such as NFPA 25 (sprinklers), NFPA 72 (alarms) and NFPA 10 (extinguishers) as adopted by each jurisdiction, and the deliverable is an inspection report the authority having jurisdiction will accept.

The tools split into two groups. Inspect Point, Uptick, ZenFire and Essential are inspection-led platforms with NFPA-based forms, deficiency tracking, quoting, scheduling and billing; BuildingReports focuses on device-level inspection and compliance reporting. ServiceTrade and BuildOps are broader commercial service platforms that run fire work alongside other commercial trades.

Inspections find deficiencies, and each one can become a repair quote, which is why Inspect Point, Uptick, Essential and ServiceTrade turn deficiencies into quotes.
verticals.feature_priorities:
Features to test for fire protection work:

Code-based inspection forms: forms that follow NFPA 25, 72, 10 and the other standards you inspect to. Inspect Point uses question sets that follow NFPA editions in the US and ULC standards in Canada, and Essential includes templates for NFPA 25, NFPA 72 and other standards.

Offline device-level capture: inspections can happen in basements and mechanical rooms without signal. Inspect Point, Uptick and Essential describe offline use; ZenFire's feature pages do not.

Deficiency to quote: Inspect Point (from its Gold plan), Uptick, Essential and ServiceTrade turn deficiencies into quotes.

Recurring inspection scheduling: due dates for each mandated inspection. Inspect Point, Uptick, ZenFire and Essential list recurring inspection scheduling.

Report submission: Inspect Point, BuildingReports, Uptick, ZenFire and Essential send reports to The Compliance Engine.

Customer portal and billing: Inspect Point, Uptick, Essential and ServiceTrade include customer portals.

vertical_faqs.q: What software do fire protection contractors use?
vertical_faqs.a: Fire contractors can choose dedicated fire and life-safety platforms or broader commercial ones. Inspect Point, Uptick, ZenFire and Essential are inspection-led platforms built around NFPA forms, deficiency tracking, scheduling and billing; BuildingReports specializes in device-level compliance reporting. Contractors whose fire work sits alongside other commercial trades can use a broader platform such as ServiceTrade or BuildOps.

vertical_faqs.q: How much does fire inspection software cost?
vertical_faqs.a: Inspect Point, BuildingReports, Uptick, ZenFire and Essential publish no prices and quote after a demo, as do ServiceTrade and BuildOps. Uptick charges a monthly fee per desk and field user, with free customer and subcontractor logins; Essential charges only for technician users, with office users free and no lock-in contract; ZenFire quotes by technician-count band and offers a 14-day free trial; Inspect Point quotes plans starting at three technicians; BuildingReports licenses its ScanSeries apps one at a time or as a suite. Get quotes on the same basis and confirm support and onboarding terms in writing.

vertical_faqs.q: Why do NFPA-compliant forms matter so much?
vertical_faqs.a: Fire and life-safety inspections follow codes (NFPA 25 for sprinklers, NFPA 72 for alarms, NFPA 10 for extinguishers and others) as adopted by each jurisdiction, and the report must satisfy the authority having jurisdiction. Built-in, code-based templates help each inspection capture the required data points and produce consistent reports.

vertical_faqs.q: Should I pick an inspection specialist or a full commercial-service platform?
vertical_faqs.a: It depends on your business mix. If fire and life-safety inspection is your core, an inspection-led platform (Inspect Point, Uptick, ZenFire, Essential) or a compliance-reporting specialist (BuildingReports) is built around the NFPA workflow. If your fire division is one of several commercial trades you run, a broader platform such as ServiceTrade or BuildOps lets you manage fire work alongside the rest in one system.

verticals.name: Pressure Washing & Window Cleaning
verticals.industry_context:
Pressure washing and window cleaning are exterior cleaning jobs. When customers ask several companies for a quote, test how fast a tool produces a quote and how it follows up, not only how it schedules. Repeat work (yearly house washes, regular window cleaning) makes recurring scheduling and reminders useful too.

Lavo CRM is built only for pressure washing and exterior cleaning, with address-based instant quotes and zone-based scheduling. The Customer Factor is a CRM for window cleaners, pressure washers and other cleaning businesses at one flat price. ResponsiBid is a quoting and follow-up tool that works alongside a CRM such as Jobber, Housecall Pro or The Customer Factor rather than replacing it. General tools such as Jobber, Housecall Pro and Workiz list this work among their trades, and QuoteIQ is a multi-trade tool.

Financing note: Jobber's Wisetack financing excludes window washing businesses.
verticals.feature_priorities:
Features to test for pressure washing and window cleaning:

Fast online quotes: pricing by surface area or property, ideally from a web form. Lavo CRM quotes from a property address using property data and satellite imagery (from its Core plan), and ResponsiBid's free Startup plan includes instant website quoting.

Automated follow-up: texts and emails that keep after quotes that have not booked. ResponsiBid's follow-up sequences start on its Scaling plan, and Lavo CRM and The Customer Factor send automated follow-ups.

Online booking and recurring scheduling: Lavo CRM's online booking (route density from its Core plan) steers new jobs toward days and zones where you already work, and The Customer Factor tracks each customer's service frequency.

Review requests: Lavo CRM, The Customer Factor and QuoteIQ list review management.

How the tools connect: if you pair a quoting tool with a CRM, check the integration. ResponsiBid connects directly to Jobber, Housecall Pro and The Customer Factor.

vertical_faqs.q: What software do pressure washing and window cleaning businesses use?
vertical_faqs.a: Operators set up their software in one of three ways: a trade-specific tool such as Lavo CRM (pressure washing and exterior cleaning) or The Customer Factor (window cleaners, pressure washers and other cleaning businesses); a general field service tool such as Jobber, Housecall Pro or Workiz, or the multi-trade QuoteIQ; or one of those paired with ResponsiBid, a quoting and follow-up tool that works alongside a CRM.

vertical_faqs.q: How much does pressure washing / window cleaning software cost?
vertical_faqs.a: Lavo CRM's Starter plan is $47 a month with 2 users. The Customer Factor is $44.95 a month flat (or $449.50 a year) with unlimited employees, though it has announced a move to three tiers. QuoteIQ starts at $29.99 a month for 1 user. ResponsiBid has a free Startup plan for instant quoting; automated follow-up and CRM connections start on its $179 a month Scaling plan (Pro is $229), plus a one-time setup fee, and it runs alongside a separate CRM. Among general tools, Jobber starts at $29 a month billed annually and Housecall Pro at $59.

vertical_faqs.q: Do I need a separate bidding tool and a CRM?
vertical_faqs.a: Not necessarily. An all-in-one (Lavo CRM, The Customer Factor, QuoteIQ, or a general tool such as Jobber or Housecall Pro) can cover quoting and operations. Adding ResponsiBid on top of a CRM makes sense if you want its quoting calculator and follow-up sequences and the extra cost pays for itself in booked jobs.

vertical_faqs.q: Why does automated follow-up matter so much for these trades?
vertical_faqs.a: When a customer asks several companies for a quote, a quote that gets no follow-up can go to a competitor who follows up. Automated texts, emails and reminders follow up on every open quote without anyone having to remember. ResponsiBid is built around this follow-up, and Lavo CRM and The Customer Factor include automated follow-ups.
